item.title: AWIEF and Open Society Foundations Champion Women-Led Enterprises for Peace and Security in Africa at AWIEF 2026
item.description: The Africa Women Innovation and Entrepreneurship Forum (AWIEF) is pleased to announce its partnership with Open Society Foundations (OSF) for AWIEF 2026 , taking place on 10 and 11 November 2026 at the Cape Town International Convention Centre (CTICC). The annual AWIEF Conference, currently in its twelfth edition, is a flagship convening of entrepreneurs, investors, corporates, government, and development partners from across Africa and beyond. The partnership will take center stage during the opening plenary, Peace Dividends: Why Women-Led Enterprise Is a Security Strategy, Not Just an Economic One , exploring how women entrepreneurs contribute to economic stability, rebuild trust in communities affected by conflict, and help create the foundations for lasting peace. Across fragile and post-conflict regions, from the Sahel to the Great Lakes and the Horn of Africa, women entrepreneurs play a vital role in restoring livelihoods and rebuilding local markets. Yet their contribution to peace building and security remains overlooked and unsung. The plenary will examine how women-led businesses can strengthen community resilience, alongside the need for more effective access to capital, supportive policies and funding systems that empower their role in peace and development. Opening Plenary: Peace Dividends The discussion will be moderated by Idil Absiaye, Regional Head of Women, Peace and Security (WPS) Policy at UN Women , and feature: Aimée Ongeso , Program Manager, Transformative Peace, Open Society Foundations. Ibrahim Mulushewa Eshete , Co-Founder and Executive Director, Center for National and Regional Integration Studies (CeNRIS), Ethiopia. Amb. Ninikanwa O. Okey-Uche, Consul General, Consulate General of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, Johannesburg. Yvette Mwanza, CEO of Kivu Mineral Resources and President of the North Kivu Chamber of Mines, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Bringing together perspectives from peace building, regional integration, diplomacy and business, the panel will explore what is working on the ground and what needs to change to better support women-led enterprises as contributors to peace and security. Through this partnership, AWIEF and OSF will spotlight the connection between women’s economic empowerment, resilient communities and sustainable peace, reinforcing the importance of recognizing women entrepreneurs as not only drivers of economic growth, but also contributors to stability across Africa. The opening plenary takes place on 10 November 2026 at the CTICC, Cape Town, as part of AWIEF 2026. Registration and tickets for AWIEF 2026 Conference are available online at: https://www.awieforum.org/purchase-conference-tickets/#tickets About AWIEF AWIEF is a leading pan-African organisation advancing women’s economic inclusion through entrepreneurship, innovation and business leadership. item.title: Ubuntu 27.04 may bring a preview of the long-awaited Core Desktop
item.description: It's a few years behind schedule, but development has resumed on the desktop edition of Canonical's existing immutable IoT distro, Ubuntu Core. Engineering veep Jon Seager announced that Canonical is Accelerating Ubuntu Core Desktop on the company's Discourse forum. Even before his announcement, there was some fresh activity on the project's GitHub . The post gives some explanation of why the effort is running so late, envisions three potential use cases, and talks a little about the work that is already going on to enable it to finally happen. There's no solid timeline given, but Seager says that "over the coming release cycle" the team will be working out what needs to happen, which means that "over the coming weeks, we'll have the infrastructure ready for… daily image builds for Ubuntu Core Desktop." "Accelerating" sounds good, but with the best will in the world, it could hardly slow it down. In mid-2023 it looked like Desktop Ubuntu Core would arrive in 2024 , and at that year's Ubuntu Summit in Rīga, Latvia, it revealed more details . At the 2024 Summit, there was a talk about a KDE version – but no release. At the 2025 Summit, the Reg FOSS desk interviewed Seager and "Where's Core Desktop?" was our first question. The three roles his post discusses are the "browser-centric machine", a "developer workstation," and a "gaming machine." For this vulture, these goals imply two separate things. In general, this seems to indicate that it's wary of making something too specialized early on, then finding that it's not versatile enough for more challenging roles. Secondly, we think that the company is thinking of three specific niches that rival immutable distros have occupied successfully for years. Right now, the "browser-centric" one is filled by ChromeOS and ChromeOS Flex . We use Flex – it's pretty good, even if its days are now numbered due to the new Android-based GooglebookOS . Secondly, Fedora's Atomic editions have been around for years now – The Register first mentioned Fedora Kinoite well over five years ago. As well as Fedoras's own versions , there are also community-led distros based on the same tech, called Universal Blue . We've tried several, and while for now they offer nothing much this vulture wants, they undeniably work and they have happy users. Fedora's marketing aims at developers, and an immutable distro with containerized environments on top is harder to accidentally break with crashy work-in-progress code. Thirdly, the games-machine niche is owned by Valve's SteamOS . Although it is native to the Steam Deck – and if you're among the lucky few, the Steam Machine and Steam Frame – you are also free to run this on your own AMD-based kit . All three of these product families have been well-established for between five to ten years now. Canonical is lagging behind, and this is a subtle acknowledgement that it knows who the leaders are. item.dc:creator: Liam Proven
item.content:encoded: It's a few years behind schedule, but development has resumed on the desktop edition of Canonical's existing immutable IoT distro, Ubuntu Core. Engineering veep Jon Seager announced that Canonical is Accelerating Ubuntu Core Desktop on the company's Discourse forum. Even before his announcement, there was some fresh activity on the project's GitHub . The post gives some explanation of why the effort is running so late, envisions three potential use cases, and talks a little about the work that is already going on to enable it to finally happen. There's no solid timeline given, but Seager says that "over the coming release cycle" the team will be working out what needs to happen, which means that "over the coming weeks, we'll have the infrastructure ready for… daily image builds for Ubuntu Core Desktop." "Accelerating" sounds good, but with the best will in the world, it could hardly slow it down. In mid-2023 it looked like Desktop Ubuntu Core would arrive in 2024 , and at that year's Ubuntu Summit in Rīga, Latvia, it revealed more details . At the 2024 Summit, there was a talk about a KDE version – but no release. At the 2025 Summit, the Reg FOSS desk interviewed Seager and "Where's Core Desktop?" was our first question. The three roles his post discusses are the "browser-centric machine", a "developer workstation," and a "gaming machine." For this vulture, these goals imply two separate things. In general, this seems to indicate that it's wary of making something too specialized early on, then finding that it's not versatile enough for more challenging roles. Secondly, we think that the company is thinking of three specific niches that rival immutable distros have occupied successfully for years. Right now, the "browser-centric" one is filled by ChromeOS and ChromeOS Flex . We use Flex – it's pretty good, even if its days are now numbered due to the new Android-based GooglebookOS . Secondly, Fedora's Atomic editions have been around for years now – The Register first mentioned Fedora Kinoite well over five years ago. As well as Fedoras's own versions , there are also community-led distros based on the same tech, called Universal Blue . We've tried several, and while for now they offer nothing much this vulture wants, they undeniably work and they have happy users. Fedora's marketing aims at developers, and an immutable distro with containerized environments on top is harder to accidentally break with crashy work-in-progress code. Thirdly, the games-machine niche is owned by Valve's SteamOS . Although it is native to the Steam Deck – and if you're among the lucky few, the Steam Machine and Steam Frame – you are also free to run this on your own AMD-based kit . All three of these product families have been well-established for between five to ten years now. Canonical is lagging behind, and this is a subtle acknowledgement that it knows who the leaders are. We didn't doubt that he knows his stuff – a year ago, Seager’s blog post about The Immutable Linux Paradox went into the differences in depth. The delay in delivering an immutable desktop is not for lack of immutable-distro technology: Canonical's had that for years. It announced Ubuntu Core 16 a decade ago, and when we tried Ubuntu Core, that was the fourth release. Seager's post identifies some of the problems that have delayed its Core Desktop. One is that the 2023 preview required its own, specially modified version of the base core22 snap. Obviously, the company would prefer that it was based on the existing Core distro. He also points to some essential underlying tech that is not obvious. He mentions that the Snap Store already has over 11,000 packages, but notes that many still use weak "classic" confinement – such as VS Code. This is a problem for Core, which requires strict confinement . He also notes some less-obvious things that need to work first, including smartphone-style permissions prompting , inter-snap dependencies, content snaps and snap components . Some of the plans are ambitious, but in good ways. He discusses the need for modularity in the desktop snap packages, so that Core Desktop won’t be restricted to only GNOME. This means isolating the display manager (that is, the login screen) from the desktop, and the desktop from the browser. Here, he gives a nod to external consultancy enioka Haute Couture for its work on KDE snaps. It's still much too easy to break any ordinary desktop Linux distro. In this vulture's extensive personal experience, the Btrfs filesystem is especially vulnerable. In four years of daily-driving a Btrfs-based distro in the 20-teens, we saw more crashes due to corrupted Btrfs volumes than in the previous two decades. However, all the vendors of Btrfs-based OSes are resolute in their denial about its real problems, which means they never get fixed. SteamOS and KDE Linux both use dual read-only Btrfs partitions, which update one another ChromeOS-style. This may be the only way to battle-harden this problematic filesystem. Canonical, on the other hand, offers integrated OpenZFS. We've been using ZFS since before the COVID pandemic, and it has yet to lose a single byte of data for us. There are still blockers before Canonical can deliver a versatile, modular, desktop version of its existing immutable OS, but it's having another go. It's about time, and there is some new hope that we may start to see previews in the Ubuntu 27.04 timeframe. ®

item.title: A phone-free Yellow Wall: are Dortmund urging fans to be present or policing them?
item.description: It makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games. The battle some clubs are waging with their fans, however, is a different dilemma By all appearances, things on the Yellow Wall seemed as they always had been. The stadium announcer hollered out the first names of Borussia Dortmund’s starting lineup and the supporters responded with their last names, tens of thousands of voices bellowing as one. Dozens of black and yellow flags waved over Europe’s largest standing terrace, a mass of faces fixed on the field beneath them. And then Signal Iduna Park, sold out with 81,365 fans, roared when Max Beier’s lone goal led Dortmund to victory over Eintracht Frankfurt last Saturday, putting the home side even on points with Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga standings. Continue reading...

item.title: BattMan aims to turbocharge US batteries without robbin' critical minerals
item.description: America's national laboratories are leading a consortium to move advanced battery storage technologies from the lab into domestic manufacturing. Dubbed the Battery Manufacturing Accelerator, or BattMan (no, really), the initiative aims to bring together a bunch of national laboratories, universities, and companies to overcome barriers in scaling up new battery technologies. Novel battery storage solutions are needed for applications in the electric grid, datacenters, and electric vehicles, as electrification gradually extends across industry. Batteries have a far lower energy density than fuels such as petroleum , so the hunt for better materials never stops. Researchers also want to improve on the safety of flammable lithium-ion cells , cut production costs, speed up charging, and reduce reliance on scarce raw materials. "The advances we make today in battery manufacturing technology will determine America's energy security and economic competitiveness for decades to come,” said Audrey Robertson, assistant secretary of Energy at the Department of Energy (DoE), which is overseeing the program. Researchers continue to develop new battery materials and chemistries, yet many promising technologies face obstacles on the way from the laboratory to commercial production. According to the DoE, BattMan will tackle that problem by combining super intelligence - known outside of the Trump administration as AI - with advanced manufacturing into a coordinated, data-driven innovation ecosystem. Pacific Northwest National Laboratory leads the consortium, along with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Argonne National Laboratory and National Laboratory of the Rockies. Academic partners include the University of Washington, Binghamton University, University of Alabama, Arizona State University, and University of Michigan-Dearborn. The accelerator is also building ties with battery and materials manufacturers, and hopes to sidestep critical minerals supply problems by finding battery materials among more abundant, domestically sourced elements. ORNL is contributing its Battery Manufacturing Facility (BMF) R&D center and plans a smart test bed with advanced sensing, real-time monitoring, and data analysis to trial both wet and dry electrode manufacturing. BattMan will also introduce autonomous pilot lines that combine sensing, process monitoring and intelligent control systems to improve product quality and reduce variability in the manufacturing process. The goal is an AI-based manufacturing platform that spots production irregularities as they occur and adjusts parameters on its own to prevent defects. “The BattMan Accelerator is exactly the kind of coordinated national effort that turns scientific breakthroughs into economic and energy security advantages,” claimed distinguished R&D staff member Chins Chinnasamy, the consortium lead for ORNL. Organizations interested in becoming part of BattMan can visit the program website to learn more. ®

item.title: Big cats, unexplained lights and a floodlit eclipse — 7 skywatching 'horror stories' to keep you entertained this Halloween
item.description: null Halloween is almost upon us! To celebrate we've pulled together a series of short "skywatching horror stories" perfect for getting you in the mood for the spooky season. Granted, stargazing may not be the most hazardous of past times. But you'd be surprised how often things can go wrong. The best laid plans can be shattered by the unforeseen, unexpected phenomena can leave you scared witless, or mother nature itself can step in to remind us how little control we have over the environment around us. Many of the stories serve as a cautionary tale, while others are simply..unfortunate. Be sure to share your stories of skywatching "horror stories" in the comments below for a chance to feature in next year's Halloween coverage! An unexplained light show over France And how better to kick off our Halloween skywatching tales than with a retelling of the strange event that terrified my entire family during a trip to France, two decades ago. We had rented a house in the Charente, with few neighbors and no city lights. It was a stargazer's paradise, so each night we would sit outside as dusk's light faded to twilight. One night, we stood transfixed as an electrical storm conjured sheet lightning in the distance, when without warning a shining ball of light burst into being on the near horizon. We watched, unsettled as the yellow-red light gently descended behind a row of oaks before passing over the nearby field. An artists depiction of the path taken by ball lightning during a sighting in 1902 near the city of Nice, France. (Image credit: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) My mom fled inside, convinced that we'd seen a UFO , while my dad and brothers stood and watched as the light silently flitted between the trees before disappearing from sight around five minutes after it had appeared. We were alone in the darkness, trying to make sense of what we'd seen when a rustle in the bushes had us borderline sprinting inside, all pretences of bravery gone and images of alien greys in our heads. It was almost certainly a boar. Our best guess is that we saw some kind of rare electrical phenomenon that night, like ball lightning , which has been reported over 10,000 times throughout recorded history but is still very poorly understood. My mom maintains that we narrowly avoided being abducted. item.content:encoded: null Halloween is almost upon us! To celebrate we've pulled together a series of short "skywatching horror stories" perfect for getting you in the mood for the spooky season. Granted, stargazing may not be the most hazardous of past times. But you'd be surprised how often things can go wrong. The best laid plans can be shattered by the unforeseen, unexpected phenomena can leave you scared witless, or mother nature itself can step in to remind us how little control we have over the environment around us. Many of the stories serve as a cautionary tale, while others are simply..unfortunate. Be sure to share your stories of skywatching "horror stories" in the comments below for a chance to feature in next year's Halloween coverage! An unexplained light show over France And how better to kick off our Halloween skywatching tales than with a retelling of the strange event that terrified my entire family during a trip to France, two decades ago. We had rented a house in the Charente, with few neighbors and no city lights. It was a stargazer's paradise, so each night we would sit outside as dusk's light faded to twilight. One night, we stood transfixed as an electrical storm conjured sheet lightning in the distance, when without warning a shining ball of light burst into being on the near horizon. We watched, unsettled as the yellow-red light gently descended behind a row of oaks before passing over the nearby field. An artists depiction of the path taken by ball lightning during a sighting in 1902 near the city of Nice, France. (Image credit: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) My mom fled inside, convinced that we'd seen a UFO , while my dad and brothers stood and watched as the light silently flitted between the trees before disappearing from sight around five minutes after it had appeared. We were alone in the darkness, trying to make sense of what we'd seen when a rustle in the bushes had us borderline sprinting inside, all pretences of bravery gone and images of alien greys in our heads. It was almost certainly a boar. Our best guess is that we saw some kind of rare electrical phenomenon that night, like ball lightning , which has been reported over 10,000 times throughout recorded history but is still very poorly understood. My mom maintains that we narrowly avoided being abducted. Total(ity) disaster Our next entry comes from Space.com's Skywatching Editor Daisy Dobrijevic, who traveled all the way from the U.K. to the U.S. in the hope of seeing her first total solar eclipse , only to have totality ruined by a series of extremely unfortunate events! "My first-ever total solar eclipse experience in Rochester, New York, on April 8, 2024 , was memorable for all the wrong reasons, Dobrijovic explained. "I was attending the Rochester Museum & Science Center's ROC the Eclipse Festival, where thick clouds had completely obscured the sun . But even without seeing the eclipse itself, totality was extraordinary. An ominous darkness raced across the sky, while rusty-red hues illuminated the clouds , creating an almost apocalyptic scene. The clouds looked as though they'd been lifted straight from a Renaissance painting. The atmosphere was electric as thousands of excited spectators watched daylight disappear. We couldn't see the eclipse, but we could certainly feel it. On April 8 clouds muted the view of the total solar eclipse over Rochester, New York. (Image credit: Future/Daisy Dobrijevic) Then, about 30 seconds into totality, disaster struck. We were standing in the museum's car park when the security floodlights suddenly flickered on, automatically triggered by the darkness. The harsh artificial lighting completely shattered the otherworldly atmosphere, robbing us of our chance to experience totality's eerie darkness. Thousands of spectators erupted into boos, shouting, 'Turn off the lights!' After traveling thousands of miles for my first total solar eclipse, I'd been thwarted first by clouds, then by a car park's security lights. Talk about adding insult to injury!" The winds of misfortune Astrophotographer Dan Bartlett experienced a very different skywatching horror story after preparing his telescopes for a night of astrophotography at his home in the Eastern Sierra Mountains. Nature had other plans. A security camera captured the sickening moment that an unexpected and sustained deluge of 77-mile-per-hour winds toppled Bartlett's Celestron Rowe-AckermannAstrograph 11-inch and 8-inch telescopes, mounts, accessories and all. "A telescope owner's worst nightmare…Equal to dropping a prized eyepiece or telescope on a cement/concrete ground," Bartlett remonstrated with Space.com. "When you first see the two scopes lying side by side, no longer upright, your reaction is to stand there and stare. Quick action of prevention is well past its timeliness. Eventually you start to pick things up and assess the damage." 11-inch and 8-inch telescopes lie broken on the ground after being toppled by high winds. (Image credit: Dan Bartlett) "One might [put] me at fault for not taking down the scopes prior, and rightly so, however the scopes have survived sustained winds of 60+ mph winds over and over before," continued Bartlett. "You develop a level of complacency and no weather forecast in the days of the event predicted winds as high as was recorded. Damage done? Severe. At least the dented tube of the RASA 11 has continued to win NASA APOD after APOD since the event. Oh, I now use sandbags on a heavier mount." Bartlett continues to capture spectacular images of the night sky to this day. An uncomfortably close look at Leo High winds may be a potent adversary for the humble stargazer, but you know what else can complicate things? Literal mountain Lions, which is what American Meteor Society shooting star expert Robert Lunsford came face to face with on a stargazing outing to the western slope of Mt. Laguna, California. "I was viewing alone in the local mountains many years ago," Lunsford recounted to Space.com. "Back then I often heard what I thought were juvenile mountain lions screeching in the dark. They were never too close until one night I shone my flashlight upon a full-grown cat about fifty yards away." A mountain lion provided an unexpected element of danger to Lunsford's stargazing outing. (Image credit: Photo by DeAgostini/Getty Images) "The adrenalin was flowing big time as I kept that light on it. Luckily, it decided it wanted no part of me and headed back down the hill. Ever since then when viewing alone I sit in the bed of my truck to offer a little more sense of security." Lunsford's cautionary tale serves as a potent reminder that you should always tell a friend or family member when you head somewhere remote for a spot of stargazing. And that you should probably do a little research on the local flora and fauna before making the trip! Eyes on the stars foot in the ants Royal Observatory Greenwich astronomer Gideon Bendavid-Walker had a run in with nature at a very different scale while leading a stargazing tour through the Arkaroola Wilderness Sanctuary in the South Australian outback, under some of the darkest skies on Earth . The Milky Way shines over the Australian Outback. (Image credit: Photo by Mark Evans/Getty Images) "I was running a tour from the sparsely used 1980's Dodwell Observatory as our main telescope was out for maintenance," Bendavid-Walker shared with Space.com. "It was going beautifully. I was out in the dark with my laser pointer, guiding a rapt group around the southern sky, when I felt a nip at my ankle. Then another. Then rather a lot… I quickly discovered that I was standing on a meat ant nest. By day they're easy to spot: a little circle of gravelly sand with a hole in the middle. At night, they're invisible, and meat ants do not take kindly to their nests being stood on." A Meat Ant, also known as Iridomyrmex Purpureus. (Image credit: Laura Symes via Getty Imag

item.title: GSA left sensitive Google Drive files open to staff, contractors
item.description: A major US federal agency has repeatedly left sensitive information in its Google Drive accessible to employees and contractors who had no legitimate business need to see it, and auditors aren’t happy. The General Services Administration (GSA), which handles contracting, procurement, property management, and other elements of basic operations for federal agencies, has faced repeated findings of inadequate protection for controlled unclassified information (CUI) since at least 2014, according to a report from the agency’s Office of Inspector General. Again. Controlled unclassified information, in the US federal government's parlance, is information that isn't classified but requires protection or restrictions on its distribution under applicable laws, regulations, or government-wide policies. Access is generally limited to individuals with a legitimate government need to know. According to the OIG report, that can include things like physical security info for government buildings, personally identifiable information (PII) of government employees, and proprietary business information, all of which the GSA has left exposed. According to the report published this week, employees and contractors have approximately 2.5 million documents stored in GSA's Google Drive. “During a limited search of GSA’s Google Drive, we found 116 files containing CUI that were improperly shared with all GSA users,” the report notes. That’s a limited search, mind you, and the OIG has plenty of reason to believe there’s more than just that sitting open for anyone with access to the GSA’s Google Drive instance to sneak a look at. The OIG said that GSA is failing to properly manage the third-party tool it has in place to prevent data loss and detect CUI exposures, with annual reviews of search terms incomplete or undocumented, many relevant search terms not implemented, and a failure to enable an available optical character recognition feature that could help detect CUI in scanned documents. Additionally, the GSA was apparently “unaware of the tool’s file size limitation of 15 megabytes,” meaning that even if the GSA was properly using that tool, some large files would still be skipped. “We also found that GSA lacks: (1) an approval process for properly sharing sensitive information and (2) a standard naming convention that could more effectively prevent exposures of CUI in GSA’s Google Drive,” the OIG added. As for what was exposed … it’s not great. According to the audit, site plans for buildings in Washington, DC were part of the improperly access-controlled files, with data that includes entrances and screening techniques, as well as the location of sensitive areas, like gun lockers. A progressive collapse analysis that "describes the building’s collapse vulnerabilities, defense vulnerabilities, and critical failure locations” was also exposed. PII of government individuals was also exposed, including social security numbers, addresses, dates of birth, and contact informa
item.dc:creator: Brandon Vigliarolo
item.content:encoded: A major US federal agency has repeatedly left sensitive information in its Google Drive accessible to employees and contractors who had no legitimate business need to see it, and auditors aren’t happy. The General Services Administration (GSA), which handles contracting, procurement, property management, and other elements of basic operations for federal agencies, has faced repeated findings of inadequate protection for controlled unclassified information (CUI) since at least 2014, according to a report from the agency’s Office of Inspector General. Again. Controlled unclassified information, in the US federal government's parlance, is information that isn't classified but requires protection or restrictions on its distribution under applicable laws, regulations, or government-wide policies. Access is generally limited to individuals with a legitimate government need to know. According to the OIG report, that can include things like physical security info for government buildings, personally identifiable information (PII) of government employees, and proprietary business information, all of which the GSA has left exposed. According to the report published this week, employees and contractors have approximately 2.5 million documents stored in GSA's Google Drive. “During a limited search of GSA’s Google Drive, we found 116 files containing CUI that were improperly shared with all GSA users,” the report notes. That’s a limited search, mind you, and the OIG has plenty of reason to believe there’s more than just that sitting open for anyone with access to the GSA’s Google Drive instance to sneak a look at. The OIG said that GSA is failing to properly manage the third-party tool it has in place to prevent data loss and detect CUI exposures, with annual reviews of search terms incomplete or undocumented, many relevant search terms not implemented, and a failure to enable an available optical character recognition feature that could help detect CUI in scanned documents. Additionally, the GSA was apparently “unaware of the tool’s file size limitation of 15 megabytes,” meaning that even if the GSA was properly using that tool, some large files would still be skipped. “We also found that GSA lacks: (1) an approval process for properly sharing sensitive information and (2) a standard naming convention that could more effectively prevent exposures of CUI in GSA’s Google Drive,” the OIG added. As for what was exposed … it’s not great. According to the audit, site plans for buildings in Washington, DC were part of the improperly access-controlled files, with data that includes entrances and screening techniques, as well as the location of sensitive areas, like gun lockers. A progressive collapse analysis that "describes the building’s collapse vulnerabilities, defense vulnerabilities, and critical failure locations” was also exposed. PII of government individuals was also exposed, including social security numbers, addresses, dates of birth, and contact information. Proprietary business information was also exposed, “including proprietary research and vendor proposals with technical and pricing information.” This might not have been publicly accessible, but it’s still a shocking lapse of data control, especially given that contractors with access to the GSA’s Google Drive could potentially view proprietary information belonging to competing vendors, giving them an unfair advantage if they used it. To make matters worse, this isn’t the first time the GSA has been dinged by its own inspector general for such lousy data protection practices. According to the report, it was 2014 when the OIG first spotted such bad habits. “In August 2014, we first reported that GSA did not protect sensitive information on child care centers, courthouses, water sources, building automation systems, and security and fire alarm systems in its Google cloud computing environment,” the OIG noted. “We issued additional reports citing concerns regarding GSA’s ability to protect sensitive information in its Google environment between 2015 and 2017.” Auditors flagged another set of improperly shared Google Drive files in April 2025. While the GSA’s chief information officer agreed with the auditors’ seven recommendations to fix the problems, the report doesn't establish whether the corrective work has been completed. The GSA has been in touch to argue it never exposed anything, thank you very much. “While the audit was underway, GSA IT confirmed their protective measures prevented the identified documents from external exposure," a GSA spokesperson told The Register. " Immediately following, significant actions were taken to strengthen the protection of CUI across the agency’s Google Workspace. GSA IT is working to fully address the Inspector General’s recommendations.”® Updated at 1933 UTC with comment from GSA.

item.title: Oracle wants to bill you for every AI task, not just every seat
item.description: Oracle expects to earn more from existing application customers as it embeds AI in its enterprise software suite. Speaking at Big Red's investor day on Wednesday, Chris Leone, executive veep of application development, said Oracle will layer usage-based revenue on top of its subscription model. “The more work that gets done by AI in our system, the more revenue we will see because they're consuming AI units as that work is getting done. We don't have to add more seats in order for us to now generate more revenue,” he said. Earlier this month, Oracle revealed its Fusion Claw runtime , designed to help customers control AI agents that automate business processes. It targets ERP, finance, and supply chain management in cloud-based Fusion applications running on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). Customers will pay for more work done inside Oracle applications, and Leone said Fusion Claw will also automate work done outside of Fusion. The promise of more revenue for Oracle, and higher bills for customers, came as the company sought to reassure investors about its spending, borrowing and revenue as it chases a share of the AI market. Oracle is funding a datacenter spending spree with negative cashflow and borrowing. OCI is set to host large language model builders, notably OpenAI, alongside its own customers' workloads. Oracle spent $55.7 billion on datacenters and cloud infrastructure in fiscal year 2026, which ended in May, and plans to spend between $90 billion and $95 billion in fiscal 2027. That will require more debt. In 2027, Oracle hopes to raise around $40 billion in debt and equity, on top of the $18 billion in debt it raised in September 2025. In a notice to investors this week, Oracle said it expects fiscal 2030 revenue of $225 billion, a compound annual growth rate of 35 percent from 2026. It expects positive cash flow by the second half of fiscal 2028, with capital spending falling the following financial year. Investors reacted positively. Oracle co-CEO Mike Sicilia also told shareholders the company will use AI to help implement its software, a plan he called as important as putting AI in the software itself. He argued AI will cut implementation time, bringing existing and new customers to OCI faster and boosting revenue. "On-premises customers can now move far more easily to the cloud by leveraging the AI tool sets to automate migrations and decrease the cost and time to implement. They don't have to be Oracle customers; they can be competitive customers." Sicilia said enterprise application software users' reluctance to change had been a major "headwind" for Oracle, one he hopes AI will ease. "Our large remaining base of on-premises customers are going to start to adopt this technology quite quickly. When we move customers from on-premises to cloud, we see a multiple increase in revenue," he said. ®

item.title: Built to bend: Postgres’s inventor and a steward on what AI really needs
item.description: Michael Stonebraker introduced Postgres ® at Berkeley in 1986. Forty years later, the database he invented is a leading choice for a generation of AI projects, and he is among the sharpest skeptics of how those projects are being built. Bruce Momjian is cofounder and core team member of the PostgreSQL Global Development Group, and he works at EnterpriseDB (EDB). In upcoming episodes of AI & Data Horizons by EnterpriseDB (EDB), the Turing Award winner and MIT professor and the Postgres community advocate both make the case that the future belongs to systems that bend without breaking, and to communities that no single company controls. Zero, not 80 Stonebraker’s first exhibit is text-to-SQL, the promise that a business user can ask a question in plain English and get an answer from the warehouse. Public benchmarks such as Spider and BIRD report accuracy above 80 percent. His team tried the same thing on MIT’s own data warehouse—1,400 tables of student, faculty, building, and salary information—using real queries from its SQL log. “We got zero-percent accuracy. Not 80, not 70, not 40—zero,” he said. Adding agentic AI, retrieval, and prompt engineering lifted that level into the teens. Telling the model every table and join term reached the 30s. “Still not ready for prime time.” The reasons are the stuff of every enterprise estate. There is no training data, because the warehouse is not on the public internet. The data is idiosyncratic: among other things, MIT buildings have numbers, not names. The schema has rotted into cryptic table and column names and overlapping views. And real queries are harder than benchmark ones. His team has published its own benchmark, Beaver, and says nobody has broken out of accuracy levels in the 30-percent range. Use the model for what it’s good at The deeper problem, Stonebraker argues, is architectural. Large language models are good with text, but “what they are no good at is doing joins of structured data,” which is most of what an enterprise holds. Working with the city of Munich’s transport department, Stonebraker’s team found that answering a single citizen complaint about crosswalk timing meant combining regulations, CAD drawings, trolley schedules, and school-zone maps. Orchestrating that with a language model at the center was, he said, “ridiculously expensive.” The team’s answer, a system called Rubicon, uses models only on text, then casts the results into tables and hands the rest to a tabular engine. The orchestrator “looks like a query optimizer.” Stonebraker says it is cheaper by a factor of 10 and considerably more accurate than agent frameworks built around a model. He expects agentic AI to slide from the top of the hype cycle into the valley of despair before a more balanced view emerges. item.dc:creator: David Gordon
item.content:encoded: Michael Stonebraker introduced Postgres ® at Berkeley in 1986. Forty years later, the database he invented is a leading choice for a generation of AI projects, and he is among the sharpest skeptics of how those projects are being built. Bruce Momjian is cofounder and core team member of the PostgreSQL Global Development Group, and he works at EnterpriseDB (EDB). In upcoming episodes of AI & Data Horizons by EnterpriseDB (EDB), the Turing Award winner and MIT professor and the Postgres community advocate both make the case that the future belongs to systems that bend without breaking, and to communities that no single company controls. Zero, not 80 Stonebraker’s first exhibit is text-to-SQL, the promise that a business user can ask a question in plain English and get an answer from the warehouse. Public benchmarks such as Spider and BIRD report accuracy above 80 percent. His team tried the same thing on MIT’s own data warehouse—1,400 tables of student, faculty, building, and salary information—using real queries from its SQL log. “We got zero-percent accuracy. Not 80, not 70, not 40—zero,” he said. Adding agentic AI, retrieval, and prompt engineering lifted that level into the teens. Telling the model every table and join term reached the 30s. “Still not ready for prime time.” The reasons are the stuff of every enterprise estate. There is no training data, because the warehouse is not on the public internet. The data is idiosyncratic: among other things, MIT buildings have numbers, not names. The schema has rotted into cryptic table and column names and overlapping views. And real queries are harder than benchmark ones. His team has published its own benchmark, Beaver, and says nobody has broken out of accuracy levels in the 30-percent range. Use the model for what it’s good at The deeper problem, Stonebraker argues, is architectural. Large language models are good with text, but “what they are no good at is doing joins of structured data,” which is most of what an enterprise holds. Working with the city of Munich’s transport department, Stonebraker’s team found that answering a single citizen complaint about crosswalk timing meant combining regulations, CAD drawings, trolley schedules, and school-zone maps. Orchestrating that with a language model at the center was, he said, “ridiculously expensive.” The team’s answer, a system called Rubicon, uses models only on text, then casts the results into tables and hands the rest to a tabular engine. The orchestrator “looks like a query optimizer.” Stonebraker says it is cheaper by a factor of 10 and considerably more accurate than agent frameworks built around a model. He expects agentic AI to slide from the top of the hype cycle into the valley of despair before a more balanced view emerges. Enterprises hate non-determinism: Approve a loan and reverse it on review, and “that’s called a lawsuit.” Organizations also need protection from rogue agents. The guardrails inside the database, he notes, largely exist already: decades of access control, complete logs, and triggers that can stop a transaction in its tracks. Data-heavy agents, he suggests, belong inside the data layer as user-defined functions, if the tooling to debug and version them improves. Stonebraker is equally blunt about the frontier. The models have already used the real training data on the internet, and he knows of no enterprise that will let a model train on its proprietary data. AGI, he said, is “basically marketing hype” from foundation model vendors justifying their valuations. Nobody owns it Why Postgres ? “Postgres is the intergalactic answer to open source,” Stonebraker said. Its unique feature is that “it’s not controlled by any one company.” EDB, Microsoft, Google, and others each contribute committers, and nobody steers. He dates its rise to Oracle buying MySQL, when “everybody said: vendor control.” For enterprises, that independence is the foundation of sovereignty : retaining control over how and where their data systems operate. Momjian describes the same structure from the inside. Postgres has no office, no assets, and no legal entity, yet it produces “software better than billion-dollar companies.” Its forecasting tool is the community itself, which spots needs early from China, Russia, and the United States. “We only need one person in the world to be supersmart, and that person to tell us what they think.” Built to bend Both experts describe a design philosophy that favors flexibility over the last few percent of speed. Stonebraker built Postgres to be extended, and that is why it absorbed JSON, full-text search, GIS, and now AI without a rewrite. Momjian adds a second call from the 1990s: Lean on the operating system rather than absorb it, which made Postgres a natural fit for the cloud. Momjian resists optimizations that buy 5 or 10 percent at the cost of rigidity, since a mistuned system can lose 40 percent. “If you take a Formula One car to the supermarket, there’s no place for the groceries.” The project plans on a horizon few vendors can match. “We’re looking at what would be the impact 5 years from now, 10 years from now.” What PostgreSQL 19 delivers The new release puts that discipline on show. Several previewed features, including SQL property graph queries and partition merging and splitting, were reverted, because reliability comes first. AI-assisted review is finding problems quickly; the August 2026 patch release for PostgreSQL 18 addressed 28 CVEs. What remains is practical: REPACK CONCURRENTLY for busy tables, smarter parallel autovacuum, and sequence synchronization for logical replication. Plan Advice, from PostgreSQL major contributor and committer Robert Haas, is the community’s answer to Oracle-style optimizer hints it rejected for years. “Somebody found a way of doing it that didn’t have the downsides,” Momjian said. The database as AI’s memory The two diverge on how fast AI will write SQL. Momjian expects agents to create databases and generate much of the code. Stonebraker says that will not happen inside the enterprise until data is documented, silos are opened, and the politics change. They agree on the destination. AI needs a relational system to give it permanence and memory, and, in Momjian’s words, that is “a game-changer.” Forty years on, the inventor and the steward are betting on the same database. item.title: Belgium's tax agency confirms cyberattack, pulls services offline
item.description: Belgium's finance and tax agency has pulled "several" digital services offline after a cyberattack on the organization. FOD Financiën confirmed the attack on Wednesday, saying that MyMinfin, the agency's main online tax portal, as well as other online services, are temporarily unavailable while they start the initial investigations. "This measure helps limit the risks and makes it possible to carry out the necessary technical interventions to ensure the security of our systems," it said in a public announcement. FOD Financiën added that "this has consequences for tax deadlines in the near future," referring to the October 31 extended deadline to submit tax filings for specific types of income, such as sole traders and earnings from foreign companies. The agency confirmed the deadline will be extended to November 16, by which time MyMinfin, the platform through which such filings would normally be submitted, should be back up and running. The detail offered up in the public statement reflects the early stage of the investigation; not much is known, although there is nothing to suggest data was compromised. "Data protection is a top priority for the FOD Financiën," it said. "At present, there are no indications that a data breach has occurred or that data has been compromised. This aspect is also being closely investigated and followed up. "In the meantime, a large part of our other applications remains available with full or partial functionality. We are closely monitoring the situation and doing everything we can to make the affected services available again as soon as possible." Spokesperson Francis Adyns told local news outlets that the attack was thwarted within hours, and that it was unable to gain access to applications or data. "The attack could not be sufficiently expanded within our environment to take over applications or gain access to data," he told Nieuwsblad . "Elements that were potentially infected were isolated. As a result, MyMinfin, Tax-on-web, and Biztax went offline, but the hacking was successfully stopped. "The various services must be restored in an isolated environment. This requires considerable time to realize, with the necessary caution to rule out new risks." ®

item.title: Rodman rule has been revised but the fight to keep stars in the NWSL goes on | Moving the Goalposts
item.description: Gone are the eight criteria to be a High Impact Player so clubs can spend their money on whomever they want – and the solution makes sense When Washington plays Chicago this Sunday in DC, “Rowdy Audi” will probably be full. It will also be full when the post-season starts, should they lock up their top-four position with a positive result on Decision Day. Equipped with an accessible stadium in a big city, a proud fanbase and a formidable roster rife with players qualifying for the High Impact Player (HIP) rule’s initial criteria (including Trinity Rodman, who gave the rule its moniker), the Spirit hold sway in the attendance charts. But starting next season, everyone on the Spirit will qualify for the “Rodman Rule” . So will every player in NWSL. Announced Friday, NWSL settled a grievance with the league’s Players Association, who argued that the initial criteria violated federal labor law. Continue reading...

item.title: Tunji Olowolafe Charts Three Strategies for Research Excellence at OAU at 65
item.description: At the Obafemi Awolowo University (OAU), Ile-Ife 65th anniversary celebration, Dr. Tunji Olowolafe , Founder of the Tunji Olowolafe Foundation (TOF) , called on Nigerian universities to open research to more people, test long-held beliefs with scientific rigour and carry discoveries out of the laboratory and into the economy. Speaking on the theme, Promoting Research Excellence and Innovation in Postgraduate Studies: Charting the Future, Dr. Olowolafe reframed research as the disciplined habit of correcting a nation’s course based on evidence. He described the postgraduate college as the intellectual engine room of a nation, where society sends its sharpest minds to challenge conventional wisdom and demand honest, data-driven answers. His first strategy called for opening the gates of research earlier, wider and more flexibly. He urged OAU to make its Staff Schools benchmarks for Africa, with science, technology and artificial intelligence at the core of the curriculum. He pointed to the Foundation’s Gbemisola Olowolafe Memorial Community Secondary School in Are-Ekiti, which opened in September 2025 with 100 students and now has more than 170, alongside an ICT centre teaching artificial intelligence, coding, graphic design and Mandarin, with instructors teaching live from Beijing through a Starlink connection. “The postgraduate researchers of 2040 are sitting in primary classrooms today,” he said. He also questioned whether every road to postgraduate research must run through a four-year degree, inviting universities to recognize prior learning and demonstrated expertise without lowering standards. With only about one million of the two million UTME candidates admitted in 2025, he argued that flexible, digital study must become the standard model, since a digital campus needs no physical acreage. This builds on the Foundation’s Project Digi-Teach, which is training academic staff at Ekiti State University (EKSU) for digital proficiency. His second strategy urged researchers to test what society believes. Rather than dismissing indigenous knowledge without investigation or defending it without validation, he called for rigorous testing, citing Chinese scientist Tu Youyou , whose study of a centuries-old herbal remedy produced the malaria treatment artemisinin and a Nobel Prize. He extended the same principle to national history, including sensitive chapters such as the Civil War. “She neither rejected tradition nor accepted it. She tested it,” he said. The third strategy focused on pushing research out of the laboratory and directly into the economy. Dr. Olowolafe advocated university promotion structures that reward patents, commercial products and solved industrial problems alongside traditional journal publications. “Research is complete only when it leaves the laboratory and improves lives,” he said. item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.content:encoded: At the Obafemi Awolowo University (OAU), Ile-Ife 65th anniversary celebration, Dr. Tunji Olowolafe , Founder of the Tunji Olowolafe Foundation (TOF) , called on Nigerian universities to open research to more people, test long-held beliefs with scientific rigour and carry discoveries out of the laboratory and into the economy. Speaking on the theme, Promoting Research Excellence and Innovation in Postgraduate Studies: Charting the Future, Dr. Olowolafe reframed research as the disciplined habit of correcting a nation’s course based on evidence. He described the postgraduate college as the intellectual engine room of a nation, where society sends its sharpest minds to challenge conventional wisdom and demand honest, data-driven answers. His first strategy called for opening the gates of research earlier, wider and more flexibly. He urged OAU to make its Staff Schools benchmarks for Africa, with science, technology and artificial intelligence at the core of the curriculum. He pointed to the Foundation’s Gbemisola Olowolafe Memorial Community Secondary School in Are-Ekiti, which opened in September 2025 with 100 students and now has more than 170, alongside an ICT centre teaching artificial intelligence, coding, graphic design and Mandarin, with instructors teaching live from Beijing through a Starlink connection. “The postgraduate researchers of 2040 are sitting in primary classrooms today,” he said. He also questioned whether every road to postgraduate research must run through a four-year degree, inviting universities to recognize prior learning and demonstrated expertise without lowering standards. With only about one million of the two million UTME candidates admitted in 2025, he argued that flexible, digital study must become the standard model, since a digital campus needs no physical acreage. This builds on the Foundation’s Project Digi-Teach, which is training academic staff at Ekiti State University (EKSU) for digital proficiency. His second strategy urged researchers to test what society believes. Rather than dismissing indigenous knowledge without investigation or defending it without validation, he called for rigorous testing, citing Chinese scientist Tu Youyou , whose study of a centuries-old herbal remedy produced the malaria treatment artemisinin and a Nobel Prize. He extended the same principle to national history, including sensitive chapters such as the Civil War. “She neither rejected tradition nor accepted it. She tested it,” he said. The third strategy focused on pushing research out of the laboratory and directly into the economy. Dr. Olowolafe advocated university promotion structures that reward patents, commercial products and solved industrial problems alongside traditional journal publications. “Research is complete only when it leaves the laboratory and improves lives,” he said. Pointing to OAU’s exceptional tech pedigree, including Flutterwave and Moniepoint founded by its graduates, he challenged the global alumni community to scale up their financial, institutional and mentorship support for research tenfold. To support this vision, the Foundation will install a solar power system for the Postgraduate College, provide a virtual learning and oral defense facility and modernize the College Boardroom. TOF will also fund pilot studies on a case-by-case basis and sponsor training in grant writing and donor compliance, working with OAU’s Central Office of Research and Advancement Office. “Our ambition must go beyond providing infrastructure to building institutions that can generate knowledge and attract global research funding. By strengthening the capacity of our universities, we can expand opportunities for our people and position Nigeria to compete more effectively in the global knowledge economy,” he added. Through these ideas and commitments, the Tunji Olowolafe Foundation continues to advance its broader ambition of strengthening the institutions, skills and opportunities that support Nigeria’s long-term development. Its work across education, digital learning and research capacity reflects a sustained commitment to equipping institutions and the next generation with the tools to compete and thrive in an increasingly knowledge-driven world. item.title: Ghostly Cat’s Head Nebula lurks within sight of Hubble and Webb
item.description: The NASA/ESA Hubble and the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescopes recently stared at an eerie star-forming scene within the Carina Nebula, a massive gas and dust cloud located approximately 7500 light-years away from Earth. The two telescopes offer complementary views of the shadowy form, nicknamed the Cat’s Head Nebula, which reflects the 'magical'' process of star formation. Hubble’s visible-light view shows the cat as a dark, elongated dust pillar and hints of young forming stars, while Webb’s infrared-light imagery unveils many stars and other hidden details.

item.title: The universe in the eye of a telescope | Space photo of the day for Oct. 29, 2026
item.description: null The Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope reflects the stars at the La Silla Observatory in Chile. (Image credit: J. Rodrigues/ESO) Stars shine in the vast aluminum dish of the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope (SEST) in this photograph captured by astronomer and astrophotographer José Rodrigues during a recent visit to the European Southern Observatory's La Silla Observatory in Chile. What is it? Rodrigues' image captures "airglow" infusing the night sky over La Silla with a soft orange glow, which is created as sunlight interacts with molecules in the upper atmosphere, according to the University of Lancaster . The subtle phenomenon can be seen reflected in the 15-meter (49-foot) primary dish of the SEST telescope along with the myriad stars of the Southern Hemisphere, as the dome of the ESO's 3.6-meter telescope looms in the background. Why is it incredible? "Despite knowing about its 15-meter diameter beforehand, I was amazed by its size," Rodrigues noted in the ESO image release. The SEST first opened its great eye to the universe in 1987, at which time it was the only large telescope in the Southern Hemisphere tasked with collecting submillimeter wavelengths of light that exist beyond the visible light spectrum. These specific wavelengths of light are emitted by wandering comets and colossal clouds of cold molecular dust and gas threaded throughout the Milky Way and beyond. SEST's observations improved our knowledge of ancient galaxies, star formation and so much more, with its perch 2,375 meters (7,792 feet) above sea level granting it a near unrivalled view of the heavens above. The SEST telescope was decommissioned in 2003, though its work was continued by the more capable Atacama Pathfinder Experiment (APEX) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA). With its working days over, the SEST telescope now stands as a quiet mirror reflecting the stars of the Southern Hemisphere night sky, seemingly pondering mysteries of the universe that it once tried to solve

item.title: Systemd adds support for Rust
item.description: Everyone's favorite Unix init system is adding support for the Unix world's favorite new programming language. What's the worst that could happen? Don't worry, this isn't here just yet. Agent P and his trusty team released systemd version 262 about a month ago. That means that systemd 263 is now under construction, and developer Christian Brauner announced on Mastodon that his new feature has been merged. The previous effort, which was pull request #44144, has now been split into five separate parts. Part 1 contains keyring-util and voa-util , described as "helpers for enrolling certificates into kernel keyrings." Part 2, support programs written in Rust , is the banner item. Then come a few more: bind only the headers Rust code uses , wrap the libsystemd-shared helpers systemd-keyring-setup needs , and finally, add systemd-keyring-setup . There are several important riders to the announcement, and these are spelled out in the second PR: "Rust is only used for new leaf components. Existing C code isn't ported and nothing that other components depend on is written in Rust." In other words, before anyone gets too excited, this does not indicate the start of an effort to rewrite systemd in Rust. All it means is that new systemd modules can be written in Rust. The second bullet point will be more significant for existing Rust developers: "No cargo. Everything is built with meson." Cargo is the Rust language’s package manager and build system. It's the normal way to build Rust applications, as well as to distribute modules of Rust code for other Rust developers to use. However, systemd already has a modern build system. It's called Meson and it's not unique to systemd – it is also used extensively by the GNOME project and the Mesa 3D graphics library. Meson itself is written in Python and uses Ninja to manage the compilation process. Ninja was designed to build Chrome faster , and it's also used for Android . The third stipulation is that any Rust code must not use the standard library . For those more familiar with C, this may sound extreme, but it's normal for embedded Rust programming . The project documents the system requirements. It needs Rust version 1.85 or later. That's modest: that version was released in February 2025 , and version 1.99.1 appeared earlier this month. It also calls for bindgen version 0.71.1 ( from December 2024 ) or newer, and Meson 1.4.0 ( from March 2024 ). These are relatively old versions – for instance, it's the Meson version included in Debian 13). Brauner added an interesting little coda in a second Masto post : saying that the team would have liked to support Rust in the core of systemd, but currently, Rust’s support for dynamic libraries isn't quite there yet. It's perhaps worth noting that writing systemd modules in Rust isn't the same thing at all as calling systemd from Rust code. There are several tools for doing that, and they have been around for years: for example, the systemd crate first appeared in 2015. ®

item.title: Critical launch for Vulcan as ULA targets Friday the 13th
item.description: United Launch Alliance (ULA) has set a target date for its return to flight: Friday, November 13, for a Vulcan launch. The mission will send 40 Amazon Leo satellites into orbit. A pair of BE-4 engines will power the booster, along with six Solid Rocket Boosters (SRBs). A Centaur V second stage, propelled by two RL10C-1 engines, will complete the journey to orbit and deploy the payload. The launch is the first Vulcan launch for Amazon after eight deployments with ULA's Atlas V. It is also the first since the launch earlier this year for the US Space Force in which an SRB burned through its nozzle during the ascent, treating viewers to some impressive fireworks and controllers to some likely clenched sphincters thanks to a "significant performance anomaly." In the event, the US Space Force payload successfully reached orbit, but the Vulcan was stood down while ULA conducted an investigation. This wasn't the first time a Vulcan had had issues with its SRBs. A nozzle was shed during the second launch of the rocket in 2024. Things went OK with the third launch. But another problem on the fourth trek to orbit meant a stand-down was unavoidable. The workhorse Atlas V has continued deploying Amazon Leo satellites during the Vulcan's hiatus. Another 29 were added on a July 2 launch from Space Launch Complex-41 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force station. However, Amazon booked 38 Vulcan rocket launches – quite an increase from the eight Atlas V launches ULA has already performed for Leo. It is obviously keen to add more satellites to its growing constellation. The SRBs are Northrop Grumman units, and the six Graphite Epoxy Motor (GEM) 63XL units will each provide an additional 459,600 lbs (2,044 kN) of thrust at liftoff. That's assuming nothing unexpected burns through or falls off. ULA has not detailed the results of its investigation or any changes it had to make. ULA said: "The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the solid rocket booster (SRB) anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle. To support our customers, this upcoming launch will utilize the improved nozzle design, and additional testing and analysis will continue in parallel with the mission. By flying the improved design, ULA gains valuable flight data that validates these improvements and is the most beneficial path in support of all our customers." US Space Force and Amazon are ULA's biggest customers - and Space Force will be watching. ULA came second to SpaceX in contracts awarded by Space Force for FY25 to FY29 . ®

A pair of BE-4 engines will power the booster, along with six Solid Rocket Boosters (SRBs). A Centaur V second stage, propelled by two RL10C-1 engines, will complete the journey to orbit and deploy the payload. The launch is the first Vulcan launch for Amazon after eight deployments with ULA's Atlas V. It is also the first since the launch earlier this year for the US Space Force in which an SRB burned through its nozzle during the ascent, treating viewers to some impressive fireworks and controllers to some likely clenched sphincters thanks to a "significant performance anomaly." item.title: SpaceX fires up Starship upper stage ahead of landmark Flight 15 test launch (video)
item.description: null SpaceX just checked another big box on the path to its 15th Starship test flight, which promises to be pretty epic. The company conducted static-fire tests with Starship 's Ship upper stage on Monday (Oct. 26) and Tuesday (Oct. 27), igniting its Raptor engines while the vehicle, known as Ship 42, remained anchored to the ground. "Ship 42 static fires complete. The Starship preparing for Flight 15 performed a full duration, six-engine static fire, and fired a single Raptor engine to simulate a deorbit burn," SpaceX said in a Wednesday (Oct. 28) X post that shared video of the tests. SpaceX conducts a six-engine static fire test with its Flight 15 Starship upper stage on Oct. 27, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) The Ship 42 tests come on the heels of a successful 33-engine static fire with Booster 22 , the Starship Super Heavy first stage that will conduct Flight 15. Everything therefore appears to remain on track for Flight 15, which SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk has said is targeted for sometime in November. All Starship launches are worth watching, but this one should be particularly exciting. Musk said last week that SpaceX will try to catch both Ship and Super Heavy during Flight 15, provided the company can get regulatory approval to do so. These catches are performed by the "chopstick" arms of the launch tower at Starbase, SpaceX's Starship launch and manufacturing hub in South Texas. The company has snagged Super Heavy on three Starship test flights to date but has not yet attempted a Ship capture. Double chopstick catches will be the norm on operational Starship launches, if all goes to plan. This recovery strategy will reduce the time needed to get Super Heavy and Ship ready for reflight, significantly boosting launch cadences, according to SpaceX. (Starship is designed to be fully reusable, unlike SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets, whose upper stages are expendable.) SpaceX is already riding a historic success with Starship: The megarocket reached orbit for the first time ever on Flight 14 , which took place on Sept. 28. And Ship deployed 26 of the company's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites during that flight, starting the assembly of a new broadband constellation that Musk has said will eventually consist of 100,000 spacecraft . Starlink V3 missions will therefore make up a significant percentage of Starship launches for the foreseeable future. But SpaceX also plans to use the megarocket to build an even bigger constellation in Earth orbit — Starmind , which could harbor one million of the company's AI data center satellites.

item.title: Shortlist of age checks for the UK's under-16 social media ban is out, 'some' adults will need verifying
item.description: The UK’s comms watchdog has put forward four methods of checking netizens aren't kids – dubbed highly effective age assurance (HEAA) – as it prepares for the proposed under-16 social media ban. The regulator says some adults may not need to prove their over-16-ness to social media platforms that will make inferences about their age based on previous activity, but confirmed that "many" are likely to have to undergo the same verification process. Big Brother Watch's (BBW) Director Silkie Carlo said: "This plan for a government 'social media ban' is a national ID system by the back door. Both the government and Ofcom have admitted that children will get around the ban, which means the real effect will be normalizing adults and children alike to handing over their passports just to get online." Ofcom says four methods remain from the seven it initially outlined when the Online Safety Act (OSA) came into force last year. The seven were capable of verifying whether a subject was 18 years old, but there are fewer viable options for determining the age of 16-year-olds, it said today. The methods put forward include: Photo-ID matching: Checking information displayed on identity documents and analyzing the photo against a live image of the subject taken during the verification process Banking checks: An estimated 90 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a bank account, which they would have provided their identity documents to open. The information processed by the bank can be used to verify whether someone is aged 16 or older Digital ID services: An interesting entry, given how quickly these were circumvented once the OSA age-checking requirements came into force. These third-party services analyze a person’s photo once, and if it matches the age they claim to be, let them verify their age across other services Facial age estimation: A method that even Ofcom admitted isn’t quite reliable enough to be used on its own. The regulator said that online services can use technologies to analyze a subject’s facial features to determine their age. The same technologies also have a margin of error of a few years, so online services may wish to use a second method of HEAA to verify the results of this check. The three reserved for those aged 18 and above include credit card checks (only adults can have a credit card), mobile network checks (MNOs require proof of adulthood to remove content blocks), and email checks – using a subject’s email address to make educated guesses about their age based on the other types of services with which it is registered. Ofcom acknowledged that not every 16-year-old will have a form of photo ID, which is required for all four of its HEAA methods, so they will need to acquire one in order to access online services. item.dc:creator: Connor Jones
item.content:encoded: The UK’s comms watchdog has put forward four methods of checking netizens aren't kids – dubbed highly effective age assurance (HEAA) – as it prepares for the proposed under-16 social media ban. The regulator says some adults may not need to prove their over-16-ness to social media platforms that will make inferences about their age based on previous activity, but confirmed that "many" are likely to have to undergo the same verification process. Big Brother Watch's (BBW) Director Silkie Carlo said: "This plan for a government 'social media ban' is a national ID system by the back door. Both the government and Ofcom have admitted that children will get around the ban, which means the real effect will be normalizing adults and children alike to handing over their passports just to get online." Ofcom says four methods remain from the seven it initially outlined when the Online Safety Act (OSA) came into force last year. The seven were capable of verifying whether a subject was 18 years old, but there are fewer viable options for determining the age of 16-year-olds, it said today. The methods put forward include: Photo-ID matching: Checking information displayed on identity documents and analyzing the photo against a live image of the subject taken during the verification process Banking checks: An estimated 90 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a bank account, which they would have provided their identity documents to open. The information processed by the bank can be used to verify whether someone is aged 16 or older Digital ID services: An interesting entry, given how quickly these were circumvented once the OSA age-checking requirements came into force. These third-party services analyze a person’s photo once, and if it matches the age they claim to be, let them verify their age across other services Facial age estimation: A method that even Ofcom admitted isn’t quite reliable enough to be used on its own. The regulator said that online services can use technologies to analyze a subject’s facial features to determine their age. The same technologies also have a margin of error of a few years, so online services may wish to use a second method of HEAA to verify the results of this check. The three reserved for those aged 18 and above include credit card checks (only adults can have a credit card), mobile network checks (MNOs require proof of adulthood to remove content blocks), and email checks – using a subject’s email address to make educated guesses about their age based on the other types of services with which it is registered. Ofcom acknowledged that not every 16-year-old will have a form of photo ID, which is required for all four of its HEAA methods, so they will need to acquire one in order to access online services. It estimates that around 94 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a form of photo ID, such as a passport, driving licence, or an ID card certified by the Proof of Age Standards Scheme, and that around 150,000 have neither. BBW's Carlo added: "Hundreds of thousands of people without ID, who tend to be poorer people, and many more who don’t want to risk handing their passports over to foreign tech companies will be locked out of huge parts of the internet. "The plan will kill anonymity online, whilst the UK’s culture of speech policing is reaching a crisis point. The policy is painfully misguided, an Orwellian assault on free speech and privacy, and will make children no safer at all." 'Circumvention inevitable' Ofcom admitted that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated," as some children will find ways to bypass these age checks, no matter how fully they are implemented. It cited Australia sporadically in its announcement, a country that introduced an under-16 social media ban in December 2025, but has struggled with a large proportion of children devising ways to circumvent these checks. Ofcom said the UK government intends to adopt, but learn lessons from, Australia’s rollout, committing to implementing more robust measures that promote the ban’s aims. It said it has identified some mitigations that could be taken to counter circumvention, such as making it easier for users to report suspected underage social media users, and “using age inference models.” The regulator said it will closely monitor circumvention for the first 12 months after the ban is enforced to understand possible methods to prevent children from finding ways around the age checks. In May, nearly a year after the OSA’s age verification requirements kicked in, researchers found that the existing age checks proved largely ineffective at keeping under-18s away from adult content online. Some reported beating age checks with just a drawn-on moustache . England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, said recently that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference" to children’s ability to access potentially harmful online content. Commenting on today’s announcement , Ofcom chief exec Dame Melanie Dawes said that when the social media ban takes effect, it will take a whole-of-society approach to ensure the ban is upheld. ?This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right," she said. "It can work if social media firms do highly effective age checks properly, and we’ve set out ways that could be achieved. When it comes into force next year, we’ll be ready to take swift and firm action against any company that fails to comply. "We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions – just like alcohol laws can’t completely eradicate underage drinking – but there’ll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk. This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it’ll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play." The UK government is expected to outline the first set of regulations related to the under-16 social media ban by the end of the year, and Ofcom is in the process of developing draft guidance for platforms. ®
